ops: - *gunicorn* for an app server in both development and production
- *django-debug-toolbar* for displaying info about a request
- *ruff* is used to lint and format the code base
- Add `pages` app to render a home page
- Add `up` app to provide a few health check pages
- Log to STDOUT so that Docker can consume and deal with log output
- Extract a bunch of configuration settings into environment variables
- Rename project directory from its custom name to `config/`
- `src/config/settings.py` and the `.env` file handles configuration in all environments
- `assets/` contains all your CSS, JS, images, fonts, etc. and is managed by esbuild
- Generate favicons using modern best practices
- Use Redis as the default Cache back-end
- Use signed cookies as the session back-end
- `public/` is the static directory where Django will serve static files from
- `public_collected/` is where `collectstatic` will write its files to
- uv is used for package management instead of `pip3` (builds on my machine are ~10x faster!)
You'll need to have Docker installed.
- The `--no-build` option will only write out a new lock file without re-building your image

Containers don't have GUIs so generally the way you interact with them is via web services or you can launch into a terminal.
One of the major advantages is that the image comes mostly preconfigured.
For those looking for a script that installs native applications check out Peter Scargill's script
Docker will not run on a PiZero or A model 1 because of the CPU. It has not been tested on a Model 2. You can still use Peter Scargill's script

For those wanting to test out the script in a Virtual Machine before installing on their Pi there are some limitations. The script is designed to work with Debian based distributions. Not all the container have x86_64 images. For example Portainer does not and will give an error when you try and start the stack. Please see the pinned issue #29, there is more info there.
